title: Genesis Abraham Call and Covenant Context
aliases: Genesis 12–17 Abraham call and promise context
summary: An isolated passage-domain evidence object for Genesis 12–17: Abraham’s call and promise, movement through Canaan and Egypt, Lot separation, the Genesis 14 war and Melchizedek scene, covenant in Genesis 15, Hagar and Ishmael in Genesis 16, and covenant sign and household in Genesis 17.
historical_context: The narratives are interpreted in their ancient Near Eastern social, political, geographic, and literary settings. Comparative evidence illuminates those settings but does not independently verify Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Lot, Melchizedek, or Genesis 14 kings; lack of direct identification does not disprove the narratives.
ancient_near_east_context: Pastoral resource use, household status, city-kings, coalition warfare, covenant ritual, naming, and circumcision are treated as bounded comparisons. Nuzi texts do not provide one-to-one proof of patriarchal customs, and no discovered treaty exactly explains Genesis 15.
hebraic_worldview: The promise develops through land, offspring, blessing, name, nations, kings, covenant relationship, and sign; the narrative’s own distinctions and uncertainties are preserved.
second_temple_context: Psalm 110 and Second Temple interpretations of Melchizedek are recorded as reception history, not as the sole meaning or applicability of Genesis 14.
canonical_context: Genesis 11 provides literary context for Genesis 12’s name-making contrast. Romans, Galatians, Psalm 110, and Hebrews may illuminate reception history but are not Genesis applicability anchors in this object.
later_christian_reception: Later Christian interpretations, including Pauline use of Genesis 15:6 and Hebrews’ Melchizedek argument, are contextual reception only. No later text is indexed as direct applicability.
canonical_role: Provides direct passage-specific cultural, historical, literary, lexical, geographical, covenantal, and reception-context evidence for Genesis 12–17 only.
literary_context: Genesis 12–17 progressively develops land, offspring, blessing, name, nation, kings, covenant relationship, and covenant sign. Genesis 11 is relevant as preceding literary context for Genesis 12 but is not an applicability anchor.
covenantal_significance: Genesis 12–17 develops promise and covenant motifs through land, offspring, blessing, nations, kings, relationship, and circumcision. Ritual comparison and later canonical readings remain distinct from each chapter’s immediate claims.
original_audience: Readers of Genesis encounter the Abraham narratives as literary and theological accounts whose ancient settings require careful comparative reasoning.
historical_setting: Narrative settings include Canaan, Egypt, the Jordan plain, and an ancient city-king political world; proposed exact dates and identifications remain unresolved.

evidence_items.title: Leaving land, kindred, and father’s house
evidence_items.description: The call commands Abram to leave his land, kin group, and father’s household for a land YHWH will show; the narrative presents costly migration and kinship rupture as the setting for the promise.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The narrated wording is treated as explicit where stated; historical, lexical, compositional, and comparative interpretations are qualified in the item and source notes.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The call commands Abram to leave his land, kin group, and father’s household for a land YHWH will show; the narrative presents costly migration and kinship rupture as the setting for the promise.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The command names land, kindred, and father’s household, then directs Abram toward an as-yet-unidentified land.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: The literary movement from departure to promise is explicit; no unspoken motive for Abram’s departure is supplied.
